title: "Whenever dharma declines, I come"
hookLine: Arjuna asks how his friend could have taught the sun, and Krishna says who he really is
carry: whenever dharma declines, he comes again
last: KAMA — THE ENEMY THAT HIDES THE SELF.

lines: I TAUGHT THIS TO THE SUN.
cards: A friend you grew up with mentions, casually, that he taught this same lesson to the sun, ages ago. That's where chapter four begins. This teaching isn't new, Krishna says.

I gave it long ago to Vivasvan, the sun, who passed it to Manu, father of humankind in Hindu tradition, and Manu to the king Ikshvaku, and down it went, king to king, until over a long time it was lost.
Now I'm giving it back to you, because you're my friend. Arjuna, reasonably, says: wait. You were born recently, and the sun long before.
How could you have taught him?

teach.h: MANY BIRTHS: I KNOW THEM, YOU DON'T.
teach.b: Krishna's answer: many births have passed, for me and for you. I know them all; you don't. Then he says what he is.

teach.h: UNBORN, YET I COME INTO BEING.
teach.b: Though I am unborn, my self imperishable, lord of all beings, I come into being through my own power. Then the promise: yada yada hi dharmasya glanir bhavati bharata.

In Edwin Arnold's 1885 translation of the two verses: "When Righteousness Declines, O Bharata! when Wickedness Is strong, I rise, from age to age, and take Visible shape, and move a man with men, Succouring the good, thrusting the evil back, And setting Virtue on her seat again."
The Sanskrit ends sambhavami yuge yuge: I come into being, age after age.

teach.h: AVATARA: THE DESCENT, AGE AFTER AGE.
teach.b: This is the root of the avatara, the descent: the divine coming down into the world in a form, again and again, when things go badly wrong.
It's how Vaishnava tradition understands Rama and Krishna, and the list of Vishnu's descents: the fish, the tortoise, the boar, the man-lion, the dwarf Vamana you met at Onam, and more.
Hindu schools read these verses differently. Some hear a personal God truly taking a body out of love. Others hear the one reality appearing through its own power, never bound by it.
To both, it isn't a promise that bad times won't come.

teach.h: WHEN THE WRONG GROWS STRONG, HE RETURNS.
teach.b: It's about what happens when they do: when the wrong grows strong, the good returns. You heard this on Janmashtami, about a baby born in a prison at midnight. Now you've heard it from his own mouth.

how: Gita 4.7–4.8, yada yada hi dharmasya, is often recited and is read as a classic statement of the avatara, the divine descent; Vaishnava Hindus often read it with the ten avatars of Vishnu in mind.

o: a soul reborn into a new body
a saint who becomes a god
the divine coming down in a form

games.q: what's inside the promise — tap the pairs.
p: the sun, first to receive the teaching
the descent, the divine taking form

s: Krishna says the Gita's teaching is brand new
he says he gave it long ago to the sun, it passed king to king, and was lost.
Krishna promises bad times will never come
he promises what happens when they do: when the wrong grows strong, he comes.
Hindu schools read these verses in more than one way
some hear a personal God taking a body out of love; others, the one reality appearing through its own power.

games.q: you're Arjuna. your friend and driver says he taught this teaching to the sun, ages ago. what do you say?
o: ask how, since he was born so recently.
games.why: he asks: you were born later, the sun long before; how could you have taught him? Krishna answers with who he is, and the promise: age after age, I come.

practice: Think of a time things had gone badly wrong, in your life, your family, the world, and then something good came back you hadn't expected: a person who showed up, a kindness, a turn.
Notice you couldn't see it coming from inside the dark part. If you pray, you can hold Krishna's promise, age after age, I come; if not, hold the memory that good has returned before.

wordCard.voice: Avatara. The descent: the divine taking form in the world, again and again. Whenever dharma declines, Krishna says, I come, age after age.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Gita 4.7: whenever, indeed, of dharma. the opening of the promise.

carryVoice: Your line: whenever dharma declines, he comes again. Age after age, when the wrong grows strong. Day one hundred seventy-one, done.
